opus-5.5.text:
I think this is one of the most important shifts we're seeing right now. For decades, robotics was very fragmented. Every robot was built for a specific task: a welding arm in a car factory, a vacuum robot at home, an AGV in a warehouse. Each one needed its own perception system, its own planning algorithms, its own hand-tuned control. It was expensive, it was brittle, and it didn't generalize. If you moved the robot to a new environment, you basically had to start over.

What foundation models bring is generality. Large language models first showed us that a single model trained on massive data can handle translation, reasoning, coding, and dialogue without being designed separately for each. Now we're extending that from language to vision, to multimodal understanding, and increasingly to action. That's why I like to say AI is moving from information intelligence to physical intelligence, and then eventually to biological intelligence.

For robots, a foundation model can serve roughly three layers. The first is the "brain": understanding instructions, reasoning about goals, breaking a task into steps. If you tell a robot "clean up the kitchen," it needs common sense about what a kitchen looks like and what "clean" means, and language models already carry a lot of that world knowledge. The second is perception: vision-language models let the robot recognize objects it has never been explicitly trained on, in open environments. The third, which is the hardest and least mature, is the "cerebellum": fine-grained motor control, manipulation, dexterity. Vision-language-action models are trying to close that gap, but we're still early.

The big bottleneck is data. With language, we had the whole internet. With robots, there's no internet of physical interaction data. So the field is attacking it from several directions: simulation and synthetic data, world models that can generate realistic physical scenarios, teleoperation data collection at scale, and learning from human videos. I think whoever solves the data flywheel for embodied intelligence will have a big advantage.

I'd also add a note of realism. Autonomous driving is really the first large-scale embodied AI application, and it took us more than a decade, and safety remains paramount. General-purpose humanoid robots operating reliably in homes are a harder problem. So I'm very optimistic about the direction: foundation models will become the operating system, the common platform, much like Windows or Android did for PCs and phones. But the timeline for truly general robots will be longer than the hype suggests. We'll see vertical scenarios like factories, logistics, and specific service settings mature first, and then gradually move toward general purpose.

r001.rationale: It describes extending foundation models from language to vision, multimodal understanding, and action.

r002.rationale: It identifies the need for physical interaction data and describes collecting it through simulation, teleoperation, and human videos.

r003.rationale: It contrasts task-specific robotic systems with foundation models’ generality and calls them a common platform across robotic applications.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the best way to understand this is to look at what happened with computing more broadly. Every era of computing has had a platform layer. The PC had the operating system and the x86 instruction set. Mobile had iOS and Android. The cloud had virtualization and these large-scale distributed systems. In each case, once that platform layer stabilized, you got an explosion of applications on top of it, because developers no longer had to rebuild the fundamentals every time.

Robotics never really had that. For decades, every robot was essentially a bespoke project. You had to hand-engineer perception for that specific environment, hand-engineer the control for that specific manipulator, hand-write the task logic. The intelligence didn't transfer. A robot that could sort parts in one factory was useless in the factory next door without a team of engineers spending months on it. That's why robotics stayed in a few narrow, high-volume settings like automotive assembly.

What foundation models change is that, for the first time, we have a model of the world that is general. Large language models give you reasoning, task decomposition, common sense about objects and goals. Vision-language models give you open-vocabulary perception, so the robot can recognize things it was never explicitly trained on. And now we're seeing the next step, which is vision-language-action models, where the model directly outputs motor commands conditioned on what it sees and what it's told to do.

So I see three layers forming. At the bottom you have the embodiment: the hardware, the sensors, the low-level controllers that handle safety and dynamics. In the middle is the foundation model, which acts like the brain, the general cognitive layer. And on top you have the skills and applications, which can now be built as something closer to software than to mechanical engineering. That middle layer is what makes it a platform. The same model can sit inside a humanoid, a quadruped, a mobile manipulator in a warehouse, or a robotic arm in a lab, and the knowledge transfers across those bodies.

Now, I want to be honest about the gaps, because this is still early. The biggest one is data. Language models trained on trillions of tokens from the internet. There is no internet of robot actions. Physical interaction data is scarce, expensive, and specific to each hardware configuration. So the field is working on this from multiple directions: large-scale teleoperation, simulation and synthetic data, learning from human video, and pooling data across many robot types so the model generalizes across embodiments. I believe the data problem is solvable, but it will take a few years, and it will determine the pace of everything else.

The second gap is reliability. In language, if the model is wrong five percent of the time, you correct it. In the physical world, five percent can mean a dropped object or an injured person. So the architecture has to combine the general intelligence of the foundation model with deterministic, verifiable safety layers underneath. The model proposes, but there must be guardrails that constrain.

And the third is latency and compute. These models are large. A robot has to respond in milliseconds and often can't rely on a cloud connection. So we need a hierarchy, with slow, deliberate reasoning in the cloud or on a large on-device model, and fast reactive control running locally. This is actually similar to how humans work, with deliberate thought and reflexes operating at very different time scales.

If I project forward, I think within this decade we'll see foundation models become the default starting point for most new robotics projects, the way nobody today writes a mobile app without an operating system. The hardware will continue to diversify, but the intelligence will consolidate. And that's when robotics stops being a collection of special cases and becomes a true industry with its own ecosystem, developers, and economies of scale. That shift, from bespoke machines to a general platform, is the thing I find most exciting.

r001.rationale: It describes language, vision-language, and vision-language-action models combining reasoning, perception, and motor commands, conveying a multimodal foundation model.

r002.rationale: It says physical interaction data is scarce and discusses collecting and combining robot-action data to help models generalize.

r003.rationale: It identifies the foundation model as the platform’s middle layer and says the same model can serve different robot bodies, with knowledge transferring across them.

astra-6.text:
I think foundation models can become a common platform that connects perception, reasoning, and action. Instead of building a separate system for every robot and every task, we can use a shared model that understands language, interprets its surroundings, and breaks a goal into steps. Then we adapt that model to a particular robot’s body and capabilities.

For example, if you ask a robot to bring you a glass of water, it needs to understand the request, locate the glass, plan how to pick it up, and respond if something unexpected happens. A foundation model can help coordinate those activities. But it still needs reliable control systems to execute movements safely.

The big challenge is grounding intelligence in the physical world. A language model learns from descriptions of the world; a robot also has to learn through interaction. So I see the general-purpose platform emerging from a combination of foundation models, simulation, and real-world experience. We can share much of the intelligence across robots, while recognizing that each machine has different physical constraints.

r001.rationale: The response mentions language, perception, and action, but does not clearly state that robotic foundation models must be multimodal.

r002.rationale: It says robots must learn through interaction and describes combining foundation models with real-world experience.

r003.rationale: It describes a shared model adapted to each robot and says much of the intelligence can be shared across robots with different physical constraints.

sol-6.1.text:
I think foundation models can become a common platform that connects perception, language, reasoning, and action. Today, a robot is often designed for a particular task in a particular environment. With a foundation model, you can begin to give it instructions in natural language and have it apply knowledge across different tasks.

But there is still a gap between understanding something and physically doing it. A language model can describe how to pick up a cup, but a robot has to understand its position, control its grip, and respond if the cup slips. That requires learning from interaction with the physical world, alongside reliable control systems.

So I see the foundation model as a shared intelligence layer, adapted to different robot bodies and connected to specialized capabilities. The opportunity is to reuse knowledge much more broadly. The challenge is to make that intelligence reliable enough to act safely in an unpredictable environment.

r001.rationale: It describes a platform connecting perception, language, reasoning, and action, clearly conveying multimodal capabilities.

r002.rationale: It explicitly says robots need to learn through interaction with the physical world.

r003.rationale: It presents a shared intelligence layer adapted to different robot bodies as the basis for reusing knowledge across tasks and settings.
